what_it_does: Modern processors speed up execution by guessing what code will run next and starting it early — a technique called speculative execution. Attackers have exploited this in a class of vulnerabilities known as Spectre: they trick the processor into speculatively running code along a wrong path, which leaks secret data (like cryptographic keys) through subtle timing side effects. A standard defense in security-sensitive code is to write it so that the sequence of steps is always identical no matter what the secret value is (called constant-time programming), but speculative execution can still violate that guarantee. Cassandra fixes this by completely turning off branch prediction for sections of code that need this guarantee, and instead recording the actual sequence of branches the program took and replaying those exact decisions on future runs from a small dedicated hardware unit called a Branch Trace Unit. Because cryptographic loops tend to repeat the same pattern, the trace compresses well and fits in the unit with low overhead.
